What the business ultimately ends up with is still open. articles.summary: Microsoft's CEO says AI agents could disrupt advertising-driven business models, forcing companies like Amazon to rethink how they compete for customers.
articles.excerpt: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella predicts that the rise of AI agents is going to reshape the economics of the internet, impacting the business models of the companies that rely on advertising and what he referred to as “human web” traffic. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the tech executive argued that the shift to an agentic web could change which companies pay others for traffic and for transactions, similar to how the transition from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google did years ago. “The current aggregators who have a business model which was for the human web will get, in some sense, reshuffled,” said Nadella. “And if you were monetizing ads because of the eyeballs, you now have to probably get down to essentially maybe CPC [cost-per-click] wins; maybe it’s more transactional,” he continued. “And so if you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will.” The discussion turned to Amazon and its decision to block AI agents from accessing its retail website, preventing them from browsing its catalog and making purchases on behalf of their users. Nadella suggested that companies trying to protect their existing business models could lose out to others that are more willing to embrace the AI agents. For instance, if Amazon continues blocking agents, another shopping platform such as Shopify, could allow them, and gain an advantage. “I think this is going to be interesting,” he said, speaking to the changing models. “It’s the same thing that’s happening in other categories, right? articles.excerpt: Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post , the company announced a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations. Many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode. Google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot. The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature. Once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests. articles.excerpt: The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training ⁠ (opens in a new window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward. Since the Hugging Face incident ⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage , from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage. We use defense in depth with m ultiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene. articles.excerpt: Eight in ten (81%) wishlist purchases happen within a week of a shopper saving an item, according to new data from Visualsoft’s VS Labs , revealing a short but valuable window for retailers to turn customer interest into sales. Analysis of almost 300,000 products saved through Wysh, VS Labs by Visualsoft’s wishlist technology, found that 81% were bought within seven days of an item being saved. More than half happened even faster, with 52% of saves becoming purchases taking place on the same day. A further 28% happened between one and seven days later. Price also appears to shape the journey from interest to purchase. Products costing under £25 were almost four times more likely to convert from a wishlist than those priced between £100 and £250, suggesting that the higher the spend, the harder retailers may have to work to turn initial interest into a sale. For higher-value products, the wishlist can mark the beginning of a longer decision-making process, giving retailers an opportunity to provide the information, reassurance or experience that helps shoppers take the next step. Wishlists give retailers a really useful signal of what customers are interested in before they make a purchase. What stands out from this data is just how quickly retailers need to act on that signal. Eight in ten purchases that come from a wishlist happen within a week, and more than half happen on the same day. That gives retailers a relatively small window where a customer has shown clear interest and is actively considering what to buy. Glossy sat down with the gm and formulator behind La Roche-Posay, L’Oréal Group’s sunscreen leader, to learn how the brand is leveraging the new filter to grow awareness and sales.
articles.excerpt: U.S. sunscreen manufacturers are navigating the biggest market change in nearly 25 years. In June, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration approved its first new sunscreen filter in 25 years: bemotrizinol, or BEMT, an ingredient that’s been widely available in Europe and Asia since 2000 and 2002, respectively. The filter has been heralded online for its remarkably lightweight, smooth feel; larger molecule size; and ability to protect against both UVA, the rays that age skin, and UVB, the rays that burn skin. “We love that we now get a new tool, and it’s not just a flash in the pan because it’s the new thing on the block,” Brian Bodnar, L’Oréal Group principal scientist of photoprotection, North America, told Glossy. “It’s important that we protect against both UVA and UVB, which is a little bit more difficult when you don’t have a large UV filter toolset to use as we might have in other countries.” BEMT offers wider photo protection than U.S. filters like avobenzone or homosalate. “We [have] really lacked this middle ground [in the U.S.], right in between UVA and UVB,” he said. “It’s a wavelength area known as UVA 2, a short wavelength right in between, and BEMT helps us fill in the gap.” What’s more, BEMT is made from a larger molecule than other chemical filters available in the U.S., which means less of the formula soaks into the bloodstream, a mounting concern among some consumers who avoid endocrine disruptors or are prone to irritation from sunscreen. “It really doesn’t go into the skin almost at all in most formulations, so you don’t have to worry about that too much,” Bodnar said. Grace Riggenbach, gm of La Roche-Posay, told Glossy that BEMT allows for better hydration and a more lightweight, elegant formula, all of which the company will lean into across marketing.

articles.excerpt: Few things frustrate ecommerce businesses more than fraud, especially when ignoring it can seem like the better option. Yes, sometimes preventing fraud — software, staff time — can cost more than the crime itself, forcing merchants to balance security with expenses and customer experience. The Merchant Risk Council is a global non-profit organization for payments and fraud prevention professionals, founded in 2000. In December 2025, MRC surveyed members across 37 countries, categories, and company sizes, and received 1,278 responses. The results, published in MRC’s “ 2026 Global Ecommerce Payments & Fraud Report,” found that 29% of respondents identified minimizing operational costs as their top fraud-management priority, up from 10% two years ago. The finding suggests that stopping fraud is no longer the only objective for nearly one in three members who evidently assess whether prevention produces a financial return. Card testing, for example, involves criminals submitting stolen payment credentials to determine which ones work. Thousands of attempts can burden checkout systems and attract scrutiny from payment providers. Refund abuse creates another expense.
